newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEP approves plans for cheaper beach monitoring.
newsitem.headline: MEP approves plans for cheaper beach monitoring.

text.p: Plans to update a 21-year old EU law on bathing water will make it cheaper for governments to monitor water quality but might not make swimming safer, a European Parliament official said on Thursday.

"The directive has been improved. Safety for the swimmer will be at least at the same level while the cost (of implementing the directive) has been reduced," an assistant to Dutch Christian Democrat Doeke Eisma told Reuters.
Parliament's environment committee is currently examining a draft report by Eisma on a European Commission proposal to update a 1975 directive on bathing water quality -- COM(94)36.
Despite the member states' parlous record of compliance with the 1975 directive, Eisma's report suggests they can be trusted properly to monitor and clean up their bathing waters.

Of the 18,000 beaches in the European Union covered by the Commission's 1995 bathing water report, more than 3,000 either failed to meet EU minimum requirements on clean water or were not monitored closely enough to determine whether they complied.

Part of the problem was the list of pollutants the member states were expected to monitor was so long that in some cases they simply did not bother, according to Eisma's assistant, Gerbenjay Gerbrandy.
The Commission has made their lives cheaper and easier by dropping from the list a series of substances which it deems do not affect bathers' health directly although they do damage the environment.
These include heavy metals, cyanide, pesticides, amonia, nitrates and phosphates.
The omissions were acceptable, Gerbrandy said, because these substances should be covered by the EU's planned framework directive on water policy.
He said it was important to find a compromise between bathers' safety and the cost to the water industry of keeping lakes, rivers and coastal waters clean.

"Science provides us with information which shows for a certain standard of water quality the number of people who will fall sick. We then have to look at the cost to the water industry of preventing that sickness," he said.
Another problem with getting the member states to respect the existing directive is that it gives them too much leeway for deciding which areas they have to monitor and clean up, says Eisma's report.
The directive defines a bathing area as one where there are "a considerable number of bathers" and its definition of the bathing season is equally vague.
Eisma's report suggests using the phrase "many bathers" would be an improvement.
Gerbrandy said referring to precise figures, such as the number of bathers per square metre, was not a solution since that could exempt governments from monitoring large but uncrowded beaches.
The member states had to be trusted to be conscientious on this point, he said.
Eisma believes they cannot however be trusted to inform the Commission of abnormally high but short-lived levels of pollution.

His report calls for the deletion of a clause which allows the member states to exclude short-lived peaks of pollution from their water quality analyses if the pollution subsides within two days and if they inform Brussels.
The report also recommends introducing harmonised methods for testing water quality, in the form of a code of conduct.
